questions.question: A block of ice sits in a freezer. It holds its shape, and nothing about it seems to move at all. What are the water particles inside the ice doing?
questions.answer: Vibrating in place, packed close together
choices: Vibrating in place, packed close together
Sitting still, packed close together
Sliding past one another, close together
Flying about, far apart from one another
questions.context: The particles in a solid are packed tightly and held in fixed places, which is why the ice keeps its shape. But they are never still: each one vibrates back and forth on its own spot, even in the cold of a freezer.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade particle models teach that a solid's particles are packed tight and vibrate in place; that they sit still is the commonest mistake.

questions.question: A student pours water from a tall, narrow measuring cylinder into a wide, flat dish. The same water now spreads out into the dish's shape. What do the water's particles do that lets a liquid change its shape this way?
questions.answer: They stay close but slide past one another
choices: They stay close but slide past one another
They stay in fixed places but bend to fit
They move far apart and fly about freely
They sit still until the pouring pushes them
questions.context: In a liquid the particles stay close together, so the water keeps its volume, but they are not held in fixed places. They slide past one another all the time, so the water flows into the shape of whatever holds it.
questions.grade_note: That a liquid's particles are close together but slide past one another, so it keeps its volume but takes its container's shape, is the 6th-grade particle picture of a liquid.

questions.question: A scientist pumps all the air out of a glass jar. Then she opens a valve and lets a little gas from a tank into it, and soon the gas fills the whole jar. Why does a gas spread through every part of its container?
questions.answer: Its particles move fast and freely in all directions
choices: Its particles move fast and freely in all directions
Its particles push one another away from a distance
Its particles are drawn toward the glass walls of the jar
Its particles swell up until they fill the jar
questions.context: A gas's particles move fast in straight lines, in every direction, until they hit another particle or a wall. Nothing holds them together, so their own motion carries them into every corner of any container. They do not push one another away from a distance or get drawn to the walls; they meet only when they collide.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade units explain why a gas fills any container: its particles are far apart and move fast and freely in every direction.

questions.question: A diving tank has room for about 11 litres of water inside. At a dive shop, a pump squeezes about 2,300 litres of air into the same tank. How can so much air fit inside it?
questions.answer: Air's particles are far apart and can be pushed closer
choices: Air's particles are far apart and can be pushed closer
Air's particles shrink smaller as they are squeezed in
Air's particles join up into fewer, bigger particles
Air's particles stop moving and stack up tidily in rows
questions.context: Most of a gas is empty space between its particles, so pressing on it pushes the particles closer together, here into about a two-hundredth of the room the air took up before. The air in the tank is still a gas, its particles still on the move. Water can hardly be squeezed at all, because its particles are already in close contact.
questions.grade_note: That a gas can be compressed because of the space between its particles, while a liquid hardly can, is part of the 6th-grade particle model of the states.

questions.question: A jeweller heats a gold ring in a small furnace. The ring glows, then slumps into a shining pool of liquid gold. What happens to the gold's particles as the ring melts?
questions.answer: They break free of their fixed places
choices: They break free of their fixed places
They melt and turn soft, as the ring does
They slow down and sink into a heap
They break into smaller bits of gold
questions.context: Heat gives the particles of a solid more and more energy. At the melting point they have enough to break free of the places that held them, and the solid becomes a liquid that flows. A particle does not melt, soften or break: only the way the particles are held together changes.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade units explain melting in particles: heating gives a solid's particles enough energy to break out of their fixed places.

questions.question: A student heats a flask of water on a hot plate. The water grows hotter and hotter until bubbles form all through it, and the water slowly boils away. How are the water's particles able to leave the liquid?
questions.answer: They gain enough energy to pull away from one another
choices: They gain enough energy to pull away from one another
They split apart into hydrogen and oxygen
They swell up until they burst out of the water
They slow down and drift apart into the air
questions.context: Heating gives the water's particles more and more energy, so they move faster and faster. At the boiling point, particles all through the water have enough energy to break free of the pull of their neighbours, and they gather in bubbles of water vapour that rise and escape as a gas. Each particle stays a whole water particle, the same size as before: none splits or swells.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade particle models (NGSS MS-PS1-4) explain boiling: heating gives a liquid's particles enough energy to break away from one another and become a gas.

questions.question: A block of ice from a freezer melts into a puddle, and the puddle is then heated until it boils away as water vapour. What about the water's particles is the same in the vapour as it was in the ice?
choices: The size of each particle
The speed of the particles
The space between the particles
How tightly the particles hold together
questions.context: The water particles in the ice and in the vapour are the very same ones, and none of them grows or shrinks. When the water boils, heat gives its particles enough energy to escape the liquid and fly off as a gas. What changes from ice to vapour is how the particles move and how they are held together, never their size.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade particle model teaches that in a change of state the particles themselves stay the same and only their motion and spacing change; that particles swell when heated is a well-known mistake.

questions.question: After a hot shower, the bathroom mirror is covered in tiny drops of water. They formed from water vapour in the warm, damp air. What happened to the water particles when they reached the cool glass?
questions.answer: They slowed down and came close together
choices: They slowed down and came close together
They sped up and spread farther apart
They stopped moving and stuck to the glass
They shrank smaller and packed into drops
questions.context: The cool glass takes energy from the water vapour that touches it. The vapour's particles slow down until they cling together, close-packed as in a liquid, and drops form on the glass. This is condensation, the reverse of evaporation.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade units explain condensation in particles: cooling slows a gas's particles until they come close together as a liquid.

5473529713.why: Judge (low, clarity): 'Resting quite still' read oddly ('quite' as 'fairly'). The still-particle lure (M2) is now 'Sitting still, packed close together', as the judge proposed. Stem, key and context unchanged.

93fbb7ed37.why: Judge (low, clarity): 'The pull between the particles' used a word the unit never teaches and could be read as a fixed property of the particles, which would also stay the same. The lure is now 'How tightly the particles hold together', the contexts' own words (F16; tightly held in ice, not held at all in vapour). Stem, key and context unchanged.

6d456e6b16.why: Judge (low, tell): two lures rested on the particle-size mistake that 93fbb7ed37 keys, and the spacing half of the key was never tested. The lures are now the evaporation picture reversed ('sped up and spread farther apart', F11, F15), the still-particle mistake ('stopped moving and stuck to the glass', M2) and one size mistake ('shrank smaller', M1). Stem, key and context unchanged.

added.58fa26f8b9: Replaces the dropped ink drop (031fd0536d) on the scope's 'liquids boil', which no question keyed: boiling in particles (F13, F20, F11). The lures are documented mistakes: water split into hydrogen and oxygen by heating (M4, M6, Osborne and Cosgrove), particles swelling when heated (M1, M6, Brook et al) and the reverse of heating's effect (slowing down, F11). The scene is a flask on a hot plate, not the T1 beaker over a burner, and the key is the particles' energy, not what the bubbles hold (solids-liquids-and-gases keys that).

dropped.question: A student sets two beakers side by side, one of hot water and one of cold. She lets one drop of blue ink fall into each and does not stir. The ink in the hot water spreads through it much sooner. Why does it spread sooner there?
dropped.why: Fact-check error and judge high: in an unstirred beaker the hot-water ink drop spreads sooner mostly through convection currents, not particles bumping the ink (F21), so the key and context taught the classroom misconception. Re-keyed to 'hot water's particles move faster' it would mirror 6d456e6b16 and take the core line of the T3 unit temperature-and-moving-particles; convection itself is the T3 unit heat-on-the-move's. Replaced, as the judge proposed, by a question on boiling in particles, which the scope names and no question keyed.
